I’d like to start a conversation, if I may. It strikes me that some of the disconnect in our critiques and comments stem from different expectations we have from solving. Sometimes I am mystified by some negative comments but that could be because I have different expectations. So, I’d love to ask the community: why do you solve the NYT crosswords?

I’ll start:
I like to be challenged: I love it when a puzzle pushes me to the very edge of my competence or even a bit beyond. Of course I don’t want be totally flummoxed; but if there’s one or two squares I can’t finish with any amount of effort, that’s OK. 

I like to be amused: please, I love to laugh or be surprised by the theme, clues, or entries.

I like to be educated: I love it when there are a few bits of trivia or references that I didn’t know before and can look up and learn about (or hear about from all of you)

I like to be impressed: the most controversial, I know. But, yeah, I love to see constructors succeed in trying something that hasn’t been done before, executing a particularly tight theme well, or filling a difficult grid. It’s like admiring art.

From Norton Juster's "The Phantom Tollbooth" (1960) which I bet was a formative childhood book for some of you:

“It looks as though I’m getting nowhere,” yawned Milo, becoming very drowsy and dull. “I hope I haven’t taken a wrong turn.”
Mile after
mile after
mile after
mile, and everything became grayer and more monotonous. Finally the car just stopped altogether, and, hard as he tried, it wouldn’t budge another inch.
“I wonder where I am,” said Milo in a very worried tone.
“You’re… in… the… Dol… drums,” wailed a voice that sounded far away.
He looked around quickly to see who had spoken. No one was there, and it was as quiet and still as one could imagine.
“Yes… the… Dol… drums,” yawned another voice, but still he saw no one.
“WHAT ARE THE DOLDRUMS?” he cried loudly, and tried very hard to see who would answer this time.
“The Doldrums, my young friend, are where nothing ever happens and nothing ever changes.”
“This time the voice came from so close that Milo jumped with surprise, for, sitting on his right shoulder, so lightly that he hardly noticed, was a small creature exactly the color of his shirt.
“Allow me to introduce all of us,” the creature went on. “We are the Lethargarians, at your service.”
“I’m very pleased to meet you,” said Milo, “I think I’m lost. Can you help me please?”
“Don’t say ‘think,' It’s against the law.”

I wanted SatinS for "paint options", I was unfamiliar with TIDE OVER, and TOE THE LINE came me to very late (I don't really know what it means, figuratively).

I felt completely stumped by the plow puller, too. Ox obviously wasn't it. Finally it dawned on me! A MULE! It was a very hard entry for me - MULEs were never common in Poland, and they were never used as draft animals: Poles relied on oxen and, later, on horses.

I can never remember how one spells the Polish sfinks in English - SPHINX looks very, very weird to my Slavic eyes, an utter mishmash of a letter salad. The pronunciation of both words is essentially the same though, with just the "i" of "sfinks" sounding different (it's the "ee" of "bee").

Oh, and your UH OH (which always confuses me when it appears in puzzles) is just "o o" in Polish. However, we never really get the chance to spell it. It's one of those things people say but that are essentially never written down.

On TOE THE LINE, my understanding of the source of this, supported directly by Brewer’s Phrase and Fable, and, indirectly by Chambers Dictionary,  is that it from sporting situations. e.g. starting races c.p. “coming up to scratch”.

Of course, Nero didn't "fiddle" while Rome burnt--bowed string instruments weren't invented for another 900 years (the oldest bowed string instrument may have been the Welsh crwth, dating from before the invention of the vowel). No, he proably played the cithara, or lyre, and sang as well. Whose fault was the Great Fire of 64CE? Was it the Christians, as Nero claimed? Was it Nero, as Tacitus--who was about seven of eight when the fire occurred--claimed? Or was it the inevitable consequence of over-built, wooden slum housing ("Insulae")? I enjoyed learning the origins of the seafaring idioms.  I used to work in the parimutuel horse racing world, and there are so many phrases that came from betting on the ponies:

Win hands down - the jockey notices she's way "ahead of the pack", so can loosen her grip on the reins as they approach the finish line.

Odd-on favorite: The horse most heavily favored to win, where the payout is less than the amount bet.

Champing at the bit: an impatient horse biting down on its metal bit while waiting for the race to start.

Across the board:  betting not only to win, but also to place (2nd) and show (3rd).

Out of the gate: showing early speed when the starting gates burst open

and Dark Horse, Track Record, Inside Track, Pacemaker, Down to the Wire, Photo Finish, Neck and Neck....

An’ sure as the mizzen be third mast from the bow, this here puzzle be remindin’ me o’ those halcyon days upon the ol’ briney, when it were just cap’n Creamy Thigh Magee, first mate Smooth Sack Rogers, and young Lindy the cabin boy, along with yours truly a’course, and nary but a bottle o’ grog between us!  Arrrr mates, them were the days, when time she stood still as a buccaneer’s bunion, and all what mattered in this world or the next was a spot of rum and a day’s haul, be it bounty or booty. We sailed these seven seas nigh on two score year, lads, and never a’fore nor since was we taken in, boarded,
nor met with cutlass or musket what we couldn’t best with our very own strength under the Jolly Roger.  Be they privateer, Corsair or landlubber, we met ‘em all with cold steel and iron will, mate, and not a man among us mind you, e’re danced with Jack Ketch nor met with Davey Jones fathoms below, and you may lay to that! Things I don’t care about: 
Streaks: I have nothing to prove to anyone and they seem to benefit the site more than the user. I know they are important to many of you.

Speed of solve: I take my time and try to leisurely enjoy the puzzle. I also know many of you may feel differently.

Ego-boost: I am of course very happy that this is a skill that I do well. But I also recognize it’s a niche skill—I know many people of high IQ, or who have more intelligence than I in many areas, who just can’t do crosswords well and have no interest in practicing. So I’m not trying to prove how smart I am, it really doesn’t reflect competence in life in general.

Those are my criteria for a satisfying puzzle, what are yours? And I want everyone to feel safe here, I promise I, at least, won’t respond negatively to anything anyone has to say.

I appreciate your "likes" as well, although I don't necessarily need to be pushed "to the very edge of my competence or a bit beyond."  That's for Saturday, occasional Thursdays and Sundays and maybe a Friday now and then.  The rest of the week I have a great time without too much pushing.

But I want to defend the enjoyment I also derive from items on your "don't care" list:

The point of a streak for me is self-discipline.  I like to feel capable of organizing my life well enough to find time for the crossword every day and to stick with it until it's solved. I take satisfaction from that.  (And just because no one else should -- or does -- care what my streak is:  1592 days.)

I like to go fast, because I like to know that I can still do the puzzles as fast (and sometimes faster) than I did them a year ago, or five years ago, or ten years ago.  My averages don't change much these days, but that means they aren't going up either.

And I absolutely enjoy an ego boost.  Who doesn't?  I took on a tricky little puzzle that teased and stretched my brain a bit, and I solved it.  Yea for me!!!  

Yes, in a few minutes I'll go back to stewing about the midterms or inflation or Raleigh's recovery from back surgery (he's one of our dogs).  But right now, my ego has been mildly boosted.

That's my take on it.

@SP What a great question! I love puzzles of all kinds, I think probably for the same reasons many people do: I like the lightbulb/aha moment in some cases, in others I just like steadily getting better at certain types of puzzles and feeling myself getting smarter. 

My complaints about the NYT puzzles (which I usually try to keep minimal, and overall I try to say more positive than negative things in my comments, personally) are usually about naticks or what seem like just trivia-based crosses that can't be puzzled out logically, where if you just don't know a certain proper name, you're s.o.l. I need it to at least be figure-out-able from the crosses. 

Though I don't usually post about it myself, I also kind of agree with people who say that the puzzles are getting too easy, mainly because it just feels less enjoyable when there are fewer "aha" moments or bits of clever misdirecting wording, and I love those; they're one of the funnest aspects of puzzles to me, so when they're missing/a puzzle feels like a gimme, it's not that I hate it, but it doesn't have that magical "Oh my brain is actually capable of figuring this out" moment to it. That little epiphanic moment where everything comes together.

Today's was a good example of a puzzle with some really good AHA moments that didn't even require misdirecting wording. Loved PIPEDOWN and TIDEOVER in particular!

It’s ironic that the word “verb” is a noun in almost exactly the same way that giving a pudgy colleague the nickname “Slim” is ironic, except that the incongruity arises naturally from the principles of standard English grammar, as you noted, rather than through intentional sarcasm. It is also contingent on particular languages to which part of speech a word belongs. In Japanese, for example, the most common way of expressing “Person X likes thing Y” uses an adjective rather than a verb. It’s very easy to imagine a language where the equivalent of “verb” is indeed an intransitive verb and one would say “‘Understand’ verbs” rather than “‘Understand’ is a verb”; to someone for whom that was their native language, the English classification would be very conspicuously incongruous.

Would you not find it ironic if the head of PETA were named Butcher or Fleischmann? Sure, that incongruity would be explicable purely due to that person’s parents’ surname or whose name they took upon marriage, but it would remain incongruous. Or would you find it ironic only if it were a fictional head of the organization in a novel, intentionally chosen by the author, rather than a hypothetical one in the real world?
